lead: UBT251 is an experimental injectable peptide that activates the GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors at once. People follow it as a next-generation weight-loss peptide after semaglutide and tirzepatide, aiming at less appetite and a leaner body.

It is designed to combine the appetite and insulin effects of GLP-1 and GIP with the energy-expenditure effects associated with glucagon-receptor activation. Two 24-week phase 2 trials in China were published in 2026, and phase 3 studies are registered. It is being tested for obesity, type 2 diabetes, kidney disease, sleep apnea and fatty liver disease.

paras: It is given as a once-weekly injection and is available only inside clinical trials. Novo Nordisk holds a licence for development outside China.
Safety data are limited to early trials. The wider drug class is associated with gastrointestinal side effects. It is not approved in any jurisdiction.

angle.text: UBT251 activates GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors to reduce appetite and raise energy use, aiming at weight loss and a leaner look. Phase 2 trials have reported, and it is not an approved or prescribable drug.

lead: UBT251 is an investigational long-acting peptide that activates three receptors at once: the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon receptors. It was developed by United Biotechnology, a subsidiary of The United Laboratories International Holdings (TUL) in China, and is given as a once-weekly subcutaneous injection in trials [1][2].

Its relevance to appearance is fat loss. Drugs in the incretin class, such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, reduce appetite and body weight, and people who lose substantial fat typically see changes in the face, waist and overall body composition. UBT251 adds glucagon-receptor activity to the GLP-1 and GIP actions of tirzepatide-type drugs; the glucagon component is associated with higher energy expenditure and effects on liver fat [1]. In a 24-week phase 2 trial in adults with overweight or obesity, average body weight fell by 13.6% to 19.7% across UBT251 arms compared with 2.0% on placebo [3].

UBT251 is not approved in any jurisdiction and is not available as a prescription medicine. Published human evidence comes from a first-in-human phase 1a/1b study and two 24-week phase 2 trials in China, reported in 2026, and phase 3 trials in obesity, type 2 diabetes and obstructive sleep apnea are registered [2][3][4][5][6]. It is being studied for obesity, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obstructive sleep apnea and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) [7][8][9][10]. In March 2025, TUL announced an exclusive licensing deal with Novo Nordisk covering development and commercialisation outside China [1].

paras: No cosmetic indication exists. Interest in the compound comes from the weight-loss magnitude reported in obesity trials: people who lose a large fraction of body weight typically show reduced waist circumference and visibly leaner features, and the phase 2 obesity trial measured waist circumference and body mass index alongside weight [3].

Registered studies cover obesity, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, MASH and obstructive sleep apnea, the last in participants who do and do not use positive airway pressure therapy [7][8][9][10][5][6].

UBT251 is a chemically synthesised peptide designed to activate the GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors together [1][2]. In the wider class of triple agonists, GLP-1 and GIP signalling are associated with glucose-dependent insulin release and reduced appetite, while glucagon-receptor signalling is associated with increased energy expenditure and effects on liver fat metabolism [1]. Detailed receptor-binding data for UBT251 have not been widely published.

The first-in-human programme included a single-ascending-dose part in healthy participants followed by a 12-week multiple-ascending-dose part, with pharmacokinetics among its stated primary aims; the product is designed for weekly administration [2].

The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled first-in-human study had two parts: a single-ascending-dose trial (phase 1a) and a 12-week once-weekly multiple-ascending-dose trial in participants with overweight or obesity without diabetes (phase 1b). Safety and tolerability were the primary endpoints. UBT251 was generally well tolerated, with laboratory findings, decreased appetite and gastrointestinal adverse events the most common effects. Across the three dose groups in phase 1b, mean body weight fell by 8.96 to 13.48 kg, while the placebo group gained 1.57 kg [2].

A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 205 adults with overweight or obesity and without type 2 diabetes (59% women, aged 18 to 61). Participants received once-weekly UBT251 in one of four arms or placebo for 24 weeks. Least-squares mean percentage change in body weight at week 24 ranged from -19.7% to -13.6% with UBT251 versus -2.0% with placebo, and placebo-adjusted differences ranged from -17.7% to -11.5% (all p < 0.001). Waist circumference, body mass index, blood pressure, lipid profile and glycemic parameters also improved, and the most frequent adverse events were mild to moderate gastrointestinal symptoms. The authors concluded that the results support phase 3 evaluation [3][11].

In a second 24-week trial, 211 Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes (mean age 48.4) were assigned to four once-weekly UBT251 arms, 1 mg semaglutide, or placebo. Glycated hemoglobin fell by 1.98% to 2.16% on UBT251, compared with 1.77% on semaglutide and 0.66% on placebo. Fasting glucose, 2-hour postprandial glucose and waist circumference fell more than on placebo, and weight reduction was greater than on both placebo and semaglutide (all p < 0.05). Gastrointestinal events were the most common treatment-emergent adverse events [4][12].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed phase 2 study in chronic kidney disease, a phase 2 study in MASH, further phase 2 studies in overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes, and phase 3 programmes in obesity, type 2 diabetes (UNIGUIDE-1) and obstructive sleep apnea [7][8][13][14][9][10][5][6].

In the published trials, the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal, mostly mild to moderate in severity, along with decreased appetite and laboratory abnormalities in the phase 1 study [2][3][4]. Drugs in the GLP-1 receptor agonist class are generally associated with nausea and vomiting. Long-term safety of UBT251 is the subject of the ongoing phase 3 trials.

According to Grokipedia, the sponsor applied for clinical-trial approval in China in June 2023 and the US FDA cleared an investigational new drug application in October 2023 [1]. Grokipedia also reports that the March 2025 agreement with Novo Nordisk included an upfront payment and milestone payments potentially reaching about $2 billion, with TUL retaining rights in China, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan [1]. These deal figures come from an AI-generated encyclopedia and have not been checked against primary announcements.

UBT251 belongs to the incretin family of weight-loss peptides that includes semaglutide and tirzepatide, which are widely discussed in fat-loss and appearance communities. As an unapproved investigational compound it is not marketed anywhere, and no community discussion of UBT251 itself is documented.

timeline.event: Clinical-trial application filed in China (June) and US IND cleared (October), per Grokipedia. [1]
Exclusive licensing agreement with Novo Nordisk announced (March); phase 2 studies in obesity and type 2 diabetes begin. [1][11][12]
Phase 1a/1b and phase 2 results published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism and Cell Metabolism; phase 3 trials registered. [2][3][4][5][6]
